column52: Nineteen year old Andrew Niemann wants to be the greatest jazz drummer in the world, in a league with Buddy Rich. This goal is despite not coming from a pedigree of greatest, musical or otherwise, with Jim, his high school teacher father, being a failed writer. Andrew is starting his first year at Shaffer Conservatory of Music, the best music school in the United States. At Shaffer, being the best means being accepted to study under Terence Fletcher and being asked to play in his studio band, which represents the school at jazz competitions. Based on their less than positive first meeting, Andrew is surprised that Fletcher asks him to join the band, albeit in the alternate drummer position which he is more than happy to do initially. Andrew quickly learns that Fletcher operates on fear and intimidation, never settling for what he considers less than the best each and every time. Being the best in Fletcher's mind does not only entail playing well, but knowing that you're playing well and if not what you're doing wrong. His modus operandi creates an atmosphere of fear and of every man or woman for him/herself within the band. Regardless, Andrew works hard to be the best. He has to figure out his life priorities and what he is willing to sacrifice to be the best. The other question becomes how much emotional abuse he will endure by Fletcher to reach that greatness, which he may believe he can only achieve with the avenues opened up by Fletcher.

column39: Miles Morales as main. Great animation, cool story. A more sarcastic and laid-back approach to what they know is a predictable and 'overdone' story, so it was a really nice and fresh look at the IP of Spider-Man. Some elements of plot felt hand-picked to fit the goal of the movie (e.g., the glitches not impacting the characters during the most important fight scenes, etc.). Sometimes brushed through Aaron moments (I wish they had more time to build up family separation parts e.g., why Aaron/Miles' dad were not on good terms or just leave that out), but maybe I just want more explicit things like the rest of the movie. Fun or meaningful side characters, very few qualms with the characters they chose. I was waiting for them to go back to KingPin's backstory because it felt too short and they covered it at the end with Miles interacting in that multi-verse hole so that worked but I didn't connect to it as I thought I would. Emotional moments didn't hit like I thought they would either, between Uncle Aaron dying (more like aw dang vs. cry), OG Peter Parker's death, or KingPin flashbacks, etc. The saddest part (close to crying) was when Miles' dad was talking to him through the doorway (that relationship was well-done). Can't ask the movie to make me feel that way but expected the combination of incredible animation and good plot to bring that out of me like K-Pop Demon Hunters and other top-tier movies did. Nitpicky more than anything. Great movie. Love the music (knew the album before the movie came out) and really good song choices from their album for the movie overall.

Some good lines here and there, seemed to be more focused on plot/story lines over comedic moments, which makes the movie more serious but also flows fine (good pacing). Music is ochestral and thematic, well done here and catchy but nothing spectatular and surprised they waited until the end credits to get Randy Newman singing. Sound effects were well done (per Sarah). Would watch again, definitely should be considered great for the time, good for present day. Grasshopper motivations were evident but in little short-lived scenes during limited timeframe for movie, we wonder if they could have done more to explore the depth of the Grasshoppers to learn more about them (tactics, propoganda, etc.), other than just their explicit power over ants and the one scene in the desert bar.

column52: Three separate but parallel stories of the U.S mortgage housing crisis of 2005 are told. He believes that the US housing market is built on a bubble that will burst within the next few years. Autonomy within the company allows Burry to do largely as he pleases, so Burry proceeds to bet against the housing market with the banks, who are more than happy to accept his proposal for something that has never happened in American history. The banks believe that Burry is a crackpot and therefore are confident in that they will win the deal. Jared Vennett with Deutschebank gets wind of what Burry is doing and, as an investor believes he too can cash in on Burry's beliefs. An errant telephone call to FrontPoint Partners gets this information into the hands of Mark Baum, an idealist who is fed up with the corruption in the financial industry. Baum and his associates, who work at an arms length under Morgan Stanley, decide to join forces with Vennett despite not totally trusting him. In addition to Burry's information, they further believe that most of the mortgages are overrated by the bond agencies, with the banks collating all the sub-prime mortgages under AAA packages. Charlie Geller and Jamie Shipley, who are minor players in a $30 million start-up garage company called Brownfield, get a hold of Vennett's prospectus on the matter. Wanting in on the action but not having the official clout to play, they decide to call an old "friend", retired investment banker Ben Rickert, to help out. All three of these groups work on the premise that the banks are stupid and don't know what's going on, while for them to win, the general economy has to lose, which means the suffering of the general investor who trusts the financial institutions. That latter aspect may not sit well with Baum. Some of these assumptions may be incorrect and may be far more manipulative than they could have ever imagined, which in turn may throw curves into the process.

The first 20 minutes are such a different tone than the first movie with their choices for dialogue and plot, that we've wasted a quarter of runtime on a TV-show-esque bit. The Ellie plot feels forced and like they were out of ideas, which is weird that 4 more movies came after this. You can't introduce 3 new "main" characters (Ellie, Crash, Eddie) by the end without developing them more than just rough-housing kids and a mammoth who thinks she's a possum (that can't be all of it). Turns into a "fun" chaotic movie but without any substance. This tone of the movie hurts the Ellie backstory scene's worth completely because we haven't felt any care for her and still don't really care about her by the end to feel any emotion about her backstory. Feels like they had magic in a bottle in the first movie and misplaced the bottle. They do a lot of walking again. All mains had weak storylines, even though "last of your kind" could be such a critical thing. The underwater stuff was way too scary for a kids movie and also didn't match the tone of the rest of the film, making it feel more chaotic and out of place.

column39: Rango (Depp) as main. A frustrating movie to sit through. You cannot come into the Nickelodeon film thinking it'll be a funny comedy for kids, as the film includes scary animals, language (hell, etc.), and weird dialogue. Still efforts to offset the serious moments with potty humour, but we feel the film could do without that and just embrace its dramatic nature, which would give more credbility to the plot, villains, and others. Great music that fits the film perfectly. The dialogue is trying too hard to be both a kid's film and a drama, and this identity crisis hurts the film. Overall seemingly well-written, and the second half after the epiphany montage scene is a good transition into the climax, but the simple nature to plot and crunched themes into 1:40 made the film feel weirdly empty and purposeless. In reflection, worldbuilding was well done, but we could've used more side character development. Great character models and animation was super well done (textures, etc). This movie was seemingly set up to succeed in animation and thematic areas, but it feels like it got molded to be a kid's movie and that completely affected its value and depth as a film. Also sucks for the main character to lie and that be the main plot for the first half without him growing significantly, or proving that he would "go back", which we don't believe him when we says he's always done that. Some moments are kinda emotional because it makes you feel for the tragedy, but without more emphasis on lives of side characters, and jokes about dead dad, etc., we don't feel terribly when things happen/don't happen, which is an oversight for this type of movie. The drawls of certain characters are hard to understand sometimes (Isla Fischer maybe tried to hard on Beans). A few moments of racism and sexism that were never needed even if assuming "they would be like that".

column39: A bit cheesy meet-cute sort between Dorothy and Jerry but a cool exploration of Jerry's emotions in general. "Show me the money" is fun. Was ready to dislike the movie bc I don't like arrogant agents but this is a more sensitive look at everything and humanizes Jerry a bit, so I like it more than I thought I would. Dorothy longing for a husband but through work is kinda meh, and the racist dad plot might be realistic but annoying to watch (but I could understand the drama, and I like Jerry being inclusive/normal). At Dorothy house alone scene + changeroom scene are kinda weird but I see the drama developing. "Let's not tell our sad stories" is a good line from Dorothy. Jerry's character changes throughout the movie which is really cool, even though it's kind of an initial tragedy with Dorothy. "You complete me" is a cool reminder of what piece of the puzzle Jerry was missing (the son Ray and to see clearly through the chaos rather than actually loving Dorothy). Jerry/Dorothy mains are good in drama. What an ending! Tactical and thoughtful movie setup.

Unfortunately his opinions aren't met with enthusiasm from his superiors and after dishonorably being stripped of his high earning clients and elite status within the agency, Jerry steps out into the sports business armed with only one volatile client, Rod Tidwell (Cuba Gooding, Jr.), and the only person with belief in his abilities, Dorothy Boyd (Renée Zellweger), with the impossible task of rebuilding what he once had. Along the way, he faces the harsh truth which he'd ignored in the past and a host of hardships that he'd never faced before.

Tim can't change history, but he can change what happens and has happened in his own life-so he decides to make his world a better place...by getting a girlfriend. Sadly, that turns out not to be as easy as you might think. Moving from the Cornwall coast to London to train as a lawyer, Tim finally meets the beautiful but insecure Mary (Rachel McAdams). They fall in love, then an unfortunate time-travel incident means he's never met her at all. So they meet for the first time again-and again-but finally, after a lot of cunning time-traveling, he wins her heart. Tim then uses his power to create the perfect romantic proposal, to save his wedding from the worst best-man speeches, to save his best friend from professional disaster and to get his pregnant wife to the hospital in time for the birth of their daughter, despite a nasty traffic jam outside Abbey Road. But as his unusual life progresses, Tim finds out that his unique gift can't save him from the sorrows and ups and downs that affect all families, everywhere. There are great limits to what time travel can achieve, and it can be dangerous too.

It's the summer of 1983 in the north of Italy, and Elio Perlman (Timothée Chalamet), a precocious 17-year-old young man, spends his days in his family's 17th-century villa transcribing and playing classical music, reading, and flirting with his friend Marzia (Esther Garrel). Elio enjoys a close relationship with his father (Michael Stuhlbarg), an eminent professor specializing in Greco-Roman culture, and his mother Annella (Amira Casar), a translator, who favor him with the fruits of high culture in a setting that overflows with natural delights. While Elio's sophistication and intellectual gifts suggest he is already a fully-fledged adult, there is much that yet remains innocent and unformed about him, particularly about matters of the heart. One day, Oliver (Armie Hammer), a 24-year-old American college graduate student working on his doctorate, arrives as the annual summer intern tasked with helping Elio's father. Amid the sun-drenched splendor of the setting, Elio and Oliver discover the heady beauty of awakening desire over the course of a summer that will alter their lives forever.

column52: It's the post-World War I era. Britons Harold Abrahams and Eric Liddell are both naturally gifted fast sprinters, but approach running and how it fits into their respective lives differently. The son of a Lithuanian Jew, Harold, who lives a somewhat privileged life as a student at Cambridge, uses being the fastest to overcome what he sees as the obstacles he faces in life as a Jew despite that privilege. In his words to paraphrase an old adage, he is often invited to the trough, but isn't allowed to drink. His running prowess does earn him the respect of his classmates, especially his running teammates, and to some extent the school administration, if only he maintains what they consider proper gentlemanly decorum, which isn't always the case in their minds. Born in China, the son of Christian missionaries, Eric, a Scot, is a devout member of the Church of Scotland who eventually wants to return to that missionary work. He sees running as a win-win in that the notoriety of being fast gives him an added outlet to spread the word of God, while he sees his speed as being a gift from God, and he wants to run to honor God and that gift. This view does not sit well with his sister, Jennie Liddell, who sees his running as only taking away time from his work to God. Harold and Eric's lives do intersect in national races, but it is the one hundred meter track event at the 1924 Paris Olympics which the two men and their supporters most anticipate. Beyond the fact that Americans Charles Paddock and Jackson Scholz are favored in the event, the much anticipated head to head between Harold and Eric may be further shadowed by other issues, especially as it affects Eric's Christian beliefs.

Zack agrees since he has no option, but as time passes and Laney begins to transform, Zack begins to find her attractive. While all that falls beautifully in place, it's not your typical fairy-tale. Mickey also meets his old lover Heather, and learns more about life itself as taxi fares in the course of a summer. Francis, a young Wall Street corporate raider, unhappy in his marriage to Renee and led by his infidelity, continues his shots at Mickey throughout the film, only to find himself a plot device that lends humor and lessons about marriage and brotherhood when he meets and starts an dangerous affair with Heather, despite Mickey's warnings that Heather is a gold-digging nymphomaniac who goes through sexual partners as often as a person changes clothes. column39: Isla Fischer and Zach Galifianakis are a solid duo as the main character suburban couple, and the film does have some fun casual moments with their relationship and working through uncovering the Joneses identity, but some of the humour and dialogue is slightly distasteful and nothing is overly funny besides the setup of the couple and the idea of it. Execution is fine, modern movie elements like text chains but hit-and-miss on jokes and not as memorable or funny as it could be, without a fun side character to attach to. Jon Hamm is better written than Gal Gadot, feeling like a gender stereotype in writing though where Gadot could be a great character to bond with Fischer rather than through sex appeal. Second half of movie is better, some jokes with better taste, some better scenes, maybe the first hour could have been re-written and Gadot/Fischer scenes omitted. Hamm + Galifianakis is a good combo.

column3: Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties
column39: People that say animation is only for kids will look to films like this to prove that point. Despite attempts at witty humour and non-kid moments, this movie is depressingly childish and shallow in concept. Dialogue can be cringey and no character to support the entire movie basically until final moments. Garfield as a main character is just tough because he's hard to like. The villain Dargis is pretty good but badly-written and all animal side characters blend into the same image. Feels like there are so many half-plots happening at the same time. Surprised it took so long for the cats to find eachother, only 15-20 mins of together plot. Cool scenery in London, UK.

William (Grant) and Anna (Roberts) as main. Really interesting choice of plot and romance, makes you feel something for the character. At times, Hugh Grant's acting is a little fake, but for most of the movie you're locked in on how things go and feel for the characters. Great music choices, and great "vibe" to the film. Would rewatch, and good britishness.

Surprised it wasn't funnier, especially with such a deep cast (Bateman, Hader, Lo Truglio, Lynch, Weaver, etc.). Kind of a cool plot, but just an excuse to go on an adventure when things aren't told to us. Some dated language too :( otherwise likely above average dialogue, enjoyed the cop banter. Kinda interesting to watch overall, with stacked cast, but kind of a let down for such a strong cast. Simon Pegg runs too much for saying he has shin splints (might be a joke but they didn't prove it well). Fun twist at the end kind of, a lot of "kind-ofs"

Dr. Grace as main. WATCHED IN THEATRE 2026-04-23. Ryan Gosling was incredible. Plot was predictable at times but not as a negative mostly, but more as a satisfying reached conclusion. Music was fitting, not exceptional, good amount of times where silence/breath was important and music respected this (honourable mention to sound design in space especially with Rocky);. Good relevance for plot points to main character. Most critiques are nitpicky over large flaws and really enjoyable mix of humour with serious moments. Few moments felt out of place and well-contrasted between the two stories (past/flashbacks and present). Beautiful movie. The cinematography was incredible, there was so much intentionality with everything in the way they shot and created it. I really enjoyed the consistent themes of love and hope throughout the movie. All the characters were unique and didn't stray from who they were. Great dialogue and again intentionality throughout every piece of the movie. Thematic moments were so emotional and awesome.

Nadine (Steinfeld) as main. Basic plot but good acting within the confines of the plot by Steinfeld and Harrelson, good relationship-themed movie. Erwin sometimes overacts a bit but the rest is realistic, teen-related film. Background type of film rather than heavily focused film with normal drama which makes it realistic but not movie universe type of entertaining. 2nd half still a solid movie despite unsure where we were going plot-wise (needed some consequences/drama/action and got some real emotion and family drama). Satisfying ending.

Astro Boy as main. Quite tragic for a kid's movie, but interesting and good world-building. Pretty emotional and message-heavy. Tough to follow at times because of how severe things become but within the cartoon universe it's still cool to watch. Some funny moments. Unsure what to think, but it's in between an intellectually high-quality movie and an irrelevant misguided idea.

Kind of a weird movie. Nick (Cera) is going through tough teen moments and well-explained feelings and all, with a second version of Cera to be his confident/aggressive version. Sheeni (Doubleday) is kind of over-acting, although fine. Not really a comedy, where most moments you find pity for Nick vs. funny. Movie without talking makes you feel things which is interesting (power of silence) but kind of a weird plot. Really cool stop-motion drawing scenes. Vijay is a fun addition. Cera is a good main and can handle him as a youth, but not something I would recommend. Writing for "funny" moments aren't that funny (e.g., initial purpose of being stripped down at night, guy at dinner table with food on face). Tough to understand purpose of movie besides Nick meeting people and going through things while we watch. Sexual nature to teen-framed movie I guess makes sense but is kind of overkill. Ending doesn't make you want to cheer because you've seen flawed main make mistakes. Fitting music.

Casper and Kat as main. Surprised to see Eric Idle, great ochestral background music, dialogue is actually quite funny and cheesy. Plot is bland but slightly fun. Gives scary movie parody vibes slightly. Some jokes suck. Overall fun to watch but low quality and not rewatch worthy mostly. Dark backstory for Casper, slightly sad. Rollercoaster scene and other sets are fun. Actually big brain ending which is wild for kids movie. B-word said too much.

Very cute movie, with somewhat interesting plot despite bland nature. Funny dialogue for kids to say. Why is Donald Trump the guy's dad. Classic kids movie that I wouldn't watch that much but I understand its fun nature.
